summaries.example: Imagine your town has a playground that many people helped build. You feel proud of it and want to keep it safe and welcoming. But if the playground has a broken swing, caring about it might mean speaking up and helping fix it—not pretending everything is perfect. Philosophers ask whether love of a country should work the same way.
summaries.summary: Patriotism is often described as love of one’s country. Philosophers examine what that love includes. It may involve feeling that the country is part of who you are, caring especially about its people, and being willing to work or give something up for what you believe the country should be. Patriotism does not always mean agreeing with the government. A person might criticize the country because they want it to become fairer or live up to its best hopes. Philosophers disagree about whether patriotism is good, required, harmless, or dangerous. Critics worry that it can put “our” people first in unfair ways, encourage hostility toward other countries, or excuse bad actions. Other philosophers defend moderate forms of patriotism that allow special care for compatriots while still respecting all human beings. The entry also explains that patriotism and nationalism are not always the same. They overlap, but one distinction treats patriotism as attachment to a country and nationalism as attachment to a people understood through shared culture, ancestry, or history. The important question is not simply whether someone loves a country, but what that love permits and asks them to do.
key_ideas: Patriotism usually includes love or loyalty to a country, identification with it, and special concern for its well-being.
A patriot may feel proud when the country does something good and ashamed when it does something wrong.
Some people think patriotism can support kindness and responsible citizenship. Others worry that it can make people treat outsiders unfairly.
The entry distinguishes patriotism from nationalism in several ways. One approach focuses on whether the object is a country or an ethnic or cultural nation.
The source describes forms of patriotism ranging from unquestioning loyalty to more critical forms that expect a country to respect justice and human dignity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Patriotism affects how people understand belonging, history, citizenship, and responsibility. It can inspire people to care for public institutions and repair their country’s mistakes. It can also become harmful if loyalty is treated as permission to ignore justice or harm outsiders. Thinking carefully about patriotism helps us ask how local belonging can fit with fairness toward people everywhere.

important_terms.definition: A strong feeling of care, loyalty, and connection to one’s country, including concern for its people and future.
A country or political community that someone regards as their own.
The idea that all people should be treated with concern and fairness, not only people from our own country.
A group whose members feel connected even though most of them do not meet face to face.

questions_to_think_about: Can you care deeply about your country while also criticizing it?
Is it fair to give special help to people from your own country?
What should someone do when their country acts wrongly?
How might love of a country be different from thinking one country is better than every other country?

summaries.example: Suppose a student learns that a national policy has harmed a minority community while benefiting many other citizens. She may still identify strongly with her country, its history, and its democratic project. An extreme patriot might defend the policy simply because it serves national interests. A moderate patriot might oppose it because loyalty is limited by justice. An ethical patriot might regard correcting the injustice as part of caring for the country’s moral identity.
summaries.summary: The entry treats patriotism as a philosophical problem about definition, identity, morality, and political life. In its ordinary sense, patriotism is love of one’s country. A fuller account adds identification with the country, special concern for its well-being and compatriots, and a readiness to make meaningful sacrifices for what the country is understood to represent. This attachment can be aspirational: a patriot may oppose the government or criticize national conduct in an effort to restore the country’s better character. Patriotism must also be distinguished from nationalism, although no single distinction is universally accepted. Some accounts contrast affection with doctrine, defense with aggression, or moderate love with hostile excess. A more conceptually neutral proposal distinguishes the objects: patriotism concerns a country or polity, while ethnic or cultural nationalism concerns a people linked by ancestry, history, and cultural traits. The central normative dispute concerns whether special attachment to compatriots is morally justified. Critics argue that it is an arbitrary form of group partiality, can corrupt belief about national virtues, and can intensify conflict or support war. Defenders argue that morality may recognize legitimate special obligations, just as it recognizes some special concern for family or friends. The entry surveys several positions. Extreme patriotism subordinates morality to national interest. Robust patriotism makes national community and its historical project central to moral identity, though this may make national “large interests” resistant to criticism. key_ideas: The core of patriotism is not merely positive feeling. It involves identification with a country and special concern for its well-being and its people, potentially including sacrifice.

Patriotism and nationalism overlap, and writers distinguish them differently. A relatively clear distinction treats their objects differently: country in one case, and an ethnic or cultural nation in the other.

The moral debate concerns partiality. Critics argue that special concern for compatriots can conflict with universal justice, human solidarity, and peace. Defenders argue that morality can allow limited special obligations.
The entry separates extreme, robust, moderate, deflated, and ethical forms of patriotism. These differ in how strongly they prioritize the country and whether they permit criticism or moral limits.

Robust patriotism links moral identity to a community’s history and projects, but critics question whether it makes national interests immune from criticism and whether the nation is necessarily the primary moral community.
Moderate patriotism can be morally permissible without being morally required. Ethical patriotism makes the country’s justice, humanity, and response to past wrongdoing central.
summaries.why_it_matters: Patriotism shapes debates about citizenship, education, public sacrifice, war, national history, and international justice. Its defenders see it as a source of solidarity and motivation for sustaining common institutions; its critics fear exclusion, self-deception, and the elevation of national interest over human beings. The distinctions in the entry prevent a simple verdict. A critical, ethically focused attachment to a country may differ morally from unconditional loyalty. The issue therefore matters not only because people disagree about a feeling, but because different forms of patriotism can support very different beliefs and political actions.

important_terms.definition: Love or loyalty directed toward one’s country, involving identification with it, special concern for its well-being and compatriots, and a commitment substantial enough to permit sacrifice.
A set of beliefs and attitudes centered on a nation understood ethnically or culturally, for example through shared ancestry, history, or cultural traits.
A moral standpoint that evaluates conduct by standards meant to apply to everyone, rather than giving automatic priority to one’s own group.
A form of patriotism that permits special concern for one’s country within limits set by universal justice and concern for humanity.
A highly demanding form of patriotism that gives a country’s major interests priority over competing moral considerations.
Patriotism focused on whether a country is just and humane, including how it confronts its past and treats people beyond its borders.
A political ideal in which loyalty is directed toward a constitution, rights, laws, and democratic institutions rather than primarily toward ancestry or culture.
The standards used to assess whether beliefs are responsibly formed, including whether evidence is examined fairly and without bias.

questions_to_think_about: Does identification with a country rationally support special concern for compatriots, or is the pronoun “my” morally insufficient by itself?
Can a patriot endorse a country without distorting evidence about its achievements and failures?
What, if anything, separates a duty of citizenship from a duty of patriotism?
Does a political community need patriotic attachment to remain stable, or can shared rights and institutions provide enough solidarity?
When does criticism of one’s country count as a form of patriotism rather than opposition to it?

summaries.example: A class discovers that its school’s history display leaves out serious harms caused by the school in the past. One student says, “Our school is the best, so do not criticize it.” Another says, “Because it is ours, we should help it tell the truth and improve.” The second response is closer to a critical or moderate kind of patriotism: caring about a community can include admitting its failures.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what patriotism is, how it differs from nationalism, and whether it deserves moral approval. Patriotism is commonly called love of one’s country, but philosophers give the idea more structure. It involves a special attachment to the country, a sense that the country is part of one’s identity, concern for its well-being and for compatriots, and sometimes a readiness to sacrifice for what the country should stand for. This does not necessarily mean supporting the government. A patriot may reject current policies because they believe the country has a better project or character to recover. Patriotism and nationalism are often confused, and philosophers draw the boundary in competing ways. Some describe nationalism as more aggressive or ideological, but that can create a convenient “we are patriots, they are nationalists” double standard. A more neutral distinction says that patriotism is directed toward a country or polity, while ethnic or cultural nationalism is directed toward a nation understood through shared ancestry, history, and culture. The moral question centers on partiality: may we give our compatriots special concern while still respecting all human beings? Critics argue that patriotism can encourage biased beliefs, hostility, militarism, and unfair preference for one’s own group. Supporters argue that communities shape our moral identities and that limited special duties can coexist with universal principles. The entry distinguishes stronger and weaker forms. Extreme patriotism treats national interest as overriding justice. Robust patriotism makes the nation’s historical project central but risks placing some national aims beyond criticism. key_ideas: Patriotism is more than liking national symbols. It commonly includes belonging, concern for the country’s welfare, and willingness to make sacrifices for its important aims.
A patriot can feel pride in national achievements and shame about national wrongdoing. This does not require believing the country is better than all others.
Philosophers do not use “patriotism” and “nationalism” in one agreed way. A useful distinction focuses on whether attachment is to a country or to a culturally understood nation.
One disagreement is between universal moral concern and special concern for compatriots. Critics see national partiality as arbitrary; defenders think morality can permit some special relationships.
Some theories make patriotism unconditional, while others say loyalty must be limited by justice, peace, and concern for people outside the country.
A country may be understood as more than its government: it can include its people, institutions, history, culture, land, and hopes for the future.
summaries.why_it_matters: People use patriotism to explain why citizens should care about public institutions, remember national history, serve others, or accept sacrifices. But the same language can be used to silence criticism or excuse mistreatment of outsiders. Studying the concept helps us separate love of a country from belief that it is always right. It also raises a wider question: how can people belong strongly to a particular community while recognizing duties to humanity as a whole?

important_terms.definition: Love or loyalty toward one’s country, usually shown through identification with it and special concern for its people and well-being.
A person’s feeling that a country is part of who they are, so its achievements and failures affect their own sense of self.
Giving extra attention or loyalty to people with whom one has a special relationship, such as compatriots, rather than treating every relationship identically.
A view that moral rules should apply to people generally and should not automatically favor one’s own group.
A political or cultural attachment to a nation, especially when nation means a people connected by shared ancestry, history, or culture.
A limited form of patriotism that allows special concern for one’s country but rejects harming others or supporting injustice simply for national advantage.
Loyalty to a country understood as an unfinished project, so criticizing its government can be a way of serving its deeper aims.

questions_to_think_about: Can criticism of a country show loyalty rather than disloyalty?
Should a country’s interests ever outweigh the interests of people in other countries?
How might patriotism affect the way people judge evidence about their country’s history?
Is patriotism morally required, merely allowed, or neither?
Can shared laws and rights unite a diverse country without shared ancestry or culture?
